concepts.name: Tideglass Chandlery
concepts.description: A compact three-storey corner chandlery, approximately six metres of street frontage and seven metres deep. Cream salt-worn plaster between substantial warm oak corner posts on a pale limestone ground storey. The characteristic feature is a shallow octagonal corner bay carried by visible carved timber brackets, with a large round brass-rimmed tide dial mounted at the middle-floor bay (plain readable tide marks, no words); it is part of the wall rather than an unrelated tower. An elegant deep-teal hipped tile roof with two small dormers and a restrained copper ridge lantern, plus one narrow brick chimney. Ground-floor wraparound glazing displays a few large coils of rope, glass fishing floats and brass storm lanterns; a recessed green entrance, a simple lantern-shaped iron hanging sign and a rolled striped awning. Upper floors are occupied rooms, unevenly opened sage shutters, a small flower box, a mended curtain. Rear face: an oak loading door beneath a small tiled canopy, a compact upper delivery hatch with a short wall-mounted pulley arm, rain chain into a stone barrel and one narrow storage lean-to that is visible coherently in both views. The trade silhouette is tide clock plus light-filled lantern windows, not a lighthouse or monumental clock tower.

Asset type: one detailed architectural concept sheet for the Rootward/Sparks seaside town, for eventual 3D modelling. It must be a specific believable town building, not a generic house and not a fantasy castle.
Input image 1: approved Guildhall Square STYLE/MATERIAL/CITY-DENSITY reference only. Input image 2: approved workshop lane OUTLINE/CRAFT/COASTAL-TOWN reference only. Do not copy either scene, beacon, guild hall, workshop or composition.

In both use orthographic parallel projection, 45-degree azimuth to the walls and about 31 degrees downward elevation from horizontal, the fixed game view. Vertical lines remain parallel; no lens/perspective convergence or distorted axes. Both views must show the same entire roof and all walls down to the foundations, no cutaways, with equal scale and lighting. Arrange generous blank space between the two silhouettes and at least 7 percent clear margins at every sheet edge. Neither roof, finial, chimney, hoist, window box, base nor rear accessory may be clipped.
STYLE: finely outlined warm painted 3D concept art like the supplied town. Strong readable roof/body forms, warm dark-brown contour lines, rich painterly material detail without noisy photorealism. Cream dressed limestone, weathered plaster, honey oak joinery, iron fittings, hand-laid roof tiles, modest brass/copper mechanisms and warm amber lamps. A cared-for, lived-in seaside trades town: salt wear low on masonry, patched shutters, practical gutters, believable doors/windows and occupied upper floors. The building could stand close to neighbouring buildings in a medium-sized dense town. Do not surround it with a floating cliff, sea diorama or a whole street. A thin restrained paving/foundation footprint below each building is enough.
CONTINUITY: exactly the same footprint, storey heights, roof ridge/gables, chimney positions, rear extension, wall openings and materials across the two views, rotated not mirrored or redesigned. Distinct front and back: shop front faces the street; deliveries, gutters and useful service details are at the rear. Supported balconies, roof loads and physically attached pipes/hoists. Keep decor subordinate to architecture. No people, robots, labels, lettering, dimension arrows, grid, title, watermark or modern cars. Signs may contain a simple pictorial trade emblem only. concepts.name: Gullstitch Sail Loft
concepts.description: A long narrow three-storey sailmaker/netmaker building, about six metres frontage and nine metres deep, between the harbour lane and a small service passage. Ochre-grey limestone ground storey with wide blue-green arched plank loading doors and a pedestrian wicket. Two jettied upper storeys of warm honey timber and pale sea-salt plaster; rust-red clay tiled long gable roof with a small ventilating ridge cupola and one squat masonry chimney. A deep central sail-loft loading opening extends across the top two floors under the FRONT gable, with solid closed/open paired timber shutters and a short useful oak hoist beam under the roof. The rope runs over a visible pulley and down to a folded sail bundle; every part is mechanically attached, no massive floating crane. An identifiable narrow net-drying gallery runs down the RIGHT long side at first-floor level, its lean roof and railing supported by timber posts; several large repaired fishing nets hang in tidy curtains, not web-like clutter. Rear gable has simple regular workshop windows and an oak service door; below, an open-sided sheltered mending bench, net floats and two spool-shaped rope reels occupy the rear end of the same gallery. Weathered pale-blue shutters, a plain pictorial needle-and-sail hanging emblem, plants in one terracotta pot and inhabited attic curtains. Make the long working elevation and useful hoist the distinctive features; this is a busy town craft house, not a ruined warehouse, pirate ship or isolated fisherman cottage.

concepts.name: Lowtide Baths and Washhouse
concepts.description: A welcoming modest three-storey public bathhouse and washhouse for a coastal trading neighbourhood, compact L-shaped footprint about seven by eight metres. Warm pale-ochre plaster, thick cream limestone ground arches, faded coral upper shutters and deep sea-green doors. A tall arched street entrance is sheltered by a shallow curved copper hood with a simple wave-and-droplet ceramic emblem; narrow frosted bottle-green windows keep the ground bathing rooms private. Two upper floors of smaller occupied rooms and linen cupboards form an irregular but coherent L plan round a tiny rear wash yard. The distinctive roof is a low terracotta hipped roof broken by a broad shallow faceted green-glass rooflight over the bathing hall; frame it like real clerestory joinery, not a giant glass dome. A small rear brick boiler annex has two slender cream ceramic chimney pots; a compact riveted copper water cistern rests on its own sturdy brick piers, with one continuous pipe leading down into the boiler annex and an overflow running to a stone wash trough. A covered rear washing gallery has folded linen and one short taut laundry line, nothing floating or covering the whole facade. Include practical gutters/downpipes, a drain channel in the rear paving, a little half-open service gate, small pots of rosemary and a worn wooden bench by the street door. Show all service infrastructure clearly in the rear view while keeping the front welcoming and domestic. It must feel like a specific seaside civic amenity within an everyday street, not a grand palace, luxury spa, industrial power station or temple.

Change ONLY the RIGHT-HAND building view. The current plate mistakenly shows the SAME net-gallery side in both images. The right-hand view must instead show the genuine diagonally OPPOSITE REAR-LEFT CORNER of that very same building, so the pair reveals ALL FOUR DIFFERENT FACADES, not a repeated wall.

Read the LEFT drawing as FRONT + RIGHT wall: front is the gable with the tall shuttered sail-loading opening and hoist; right wall is the long NET-DRYING GALLERY wall. For the new RIGHT drawing, turn around the building by 180 degrees: show the BACK gable and the previously unseen LEFT long wall. - Preserve the SAME long rust-red tiled gable roof, same small teal roof-ridge ventilation cupola, same masonry chimney position relative to ridge and building ends as the LEFT reference. The front hoist remains on the distant hidden front gable, not moved to the back.
